This wizard creates a cross-tab query for summarizing table data in a spreadsheet format.

 To access the Cross-Tab wizard
 - From the Tools menu, choose Wizards , and click Query .
- In the Wizard Selection dialog box, choose Cross-Tab Wizard .

In this step, you can choose a free table or a table within a database as the source for your pivot table. You can select only fields from a single table or view. For more information, see Working with Views ([[T0]]).

 To select the fields for your cross-tab query
 - Use the Databases and Tables controls to locate and select the table you want to use.
- In the Available fields window, select three or four fields you want to use from the selected table, and use the arrow buttons to move them to the Selected fields window.

You need to choose at least three fields; one each for row values, column values, and data.

In this step, you can specify which field values will be calculated for the data. For example, if you have an Orders table that contains, among others, a field for city, a field for region, and a field for order amount, you could create a pivot table that would display in the data area, sums for all the cities, by region. At the bottom, the table will display totals for each column. At the far right, the table will display totals for each row.

 To define the cross-tab layout
 - From the Available fields list, drag a field to the Rows box. The cross-tab query will contain a row for each unique value in the field that you drag to the Rows box
- From the Available fields list, drag a field to the Columns box. The cross-tab query will contain a column for each unique value in the field that you drag to the Columns box
- From the Available fields list, drag a field to the Data box. Because this field will be summarized, generally it is best to drag a numeric field here.

If you have a large table, you might want to first create a view that contains the desired fields and then create a cross-tab query from that view.

In this step, you can determine if you want to add a subtotal column and summary information in your data. To add summary information, select the appropriate radio button (Sum, Count, Average, Max, or Min) in the Summary section. To add a subtotal column, select the appropriate radio button (Sum of data, Number of cells containing data, or Percentage of the table total) in the Subtotals section. If you do not want to add a subtotal column, select the None radio button in the Subtotals section. The totals will appear in the rightmost column of your cross-tab query results.

This step makes it possible to save and specify the use of your cross-tab query.
 **Save cross-tab query**
Saves the cross-tab query for use later.
**Save and run cross-tab query**
Saves the cross-tab query and runs it immediately.
**Save cross-tab query and modify in the Query Designer**
Saves the cross-tab query and opens it in the Query designer so you can modify it.

You can preview your cross-tab query by clicking the Preview button. To view null values, select the Display Null Values check box.

At any point after you save the cross-tab query, you can open and modify it as you would with any other query in the Query and View designers.

textos.1f84a128-0157-472f-863b-0ed5f69d2dc5#216: You can create a variety of formats for output generated from Field controls by creating a format string expression. A format string contains format codes and format templates.

Format codes apply to all the characters in the Field control expression and must be preceded by the at sign (@) in the format string. For example, you can pad a numeric value with leading zeros instead of spaces by using the format string "@L 999999".

| Format Code: | Description: | Applies to data of type: |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ! | Force text to uppercase. | Character only |
| B | Left justify . | All types |
| J | Right justify. | All types |
| I | Center justify. | All types |
| L | Leading zeros. | Numeric only |
| Z | Blank if zero. | Numeric, Date, and DateTime |
| ( | Surround negative numbers [[T0]]. | Numeric only |
| C | Appends " [[T1]]" to positive, non-zero numbers. | Numeric only |
| X | Appends " [[T2]]" to negative, non-zero numbers. | Numeric only |
| $ | Uses currency notation. | Numeric only |
| D | Use current [[T3]] setting. | All types |
| E | Display as if [[T4]] was in effect. | All types |
| [[T5]] | Display using system Long Date format. | Date |
| [[T6]] | Display using system Short Date format. | Date |
| R | Prevents non-formatting characters in the template string from replacing the corresponding character of the field expression value. When @R is used, the template string interleaves instead of overlaying . (See example below.) | Character and Numeric |
textos.1f84a128-0157-472f-863b-0ed5f69d2dc5#217:
- Numeric data is right-justified by default.
- Character and Date data are left-justified by default.
- You can use combinations of format codes. For example "@[[T0]]" will display both credits and debits on numeric data, where appropriate.

For more information about how format codes are used in form controls, see Format Property.

Format template characters apply to individual characters in the Field control expression. You can create a pattern with format template characters with each character in the template representing a character you want to display. For example, some characters in a format template alter the display of specific character types. For example, including the character "Y" in a format template for a logical expression displays the letters "Y" instead of "[[T0]]" for True and "N" instead of "[[T1]]" for False. The character "9" in a format template is a placeholder for any digit in character or numeric data. Other format template characters, such as parentheses, spaces, and hyphens, display as themselves.

For more information about format template characters, see InputMask Property.

The following examples show how format codes and format template characters work together to create the output:

| 65.43 | (999) 999-9999 | ( ) - -43 |
| "4505551023" | (999) 999-9999 | (505) 102- |
| "4505551023" | @R (999) 999-9999 | (450) 555-1023 |

[[C0]]

**alias_name**
Specifies the name of the temporary table to create. The alias_name parameter can be a name expression.
**[[T0]]**
Specifies the code page to use. For a list of code pages, see Code Pages Supported by [[T1]] .
**fname**
Specifies the name of a field in the temporary table. Each fname can be a name expression.
**[[T2]]**
Specifies a single letter or a long name indicating the field's data type.
**[[T3]]**
Specifies the width of the field specified with fname . Some data types require that you specify a value for [[T4]] .
**[[T5]]**
Specifies the number of decimal places for the specified data type. Some data types require that you specify a value for [[T6]] . The following table shows the possible values for [[T7]] , [[T8]] , and [[T9]] . [[T10]] [[T11]] [[T12]] Description W, Blob - - Blob C, Char, Character n – Character field of width n Y, Currency – – Currency D, Date – – Date T, DateTime – – DateTime B, Double – d Double G, General – – General I, Int, Integer – – Integer L, Logical – – Logical M, Memo – – Memo N, Num, Numeric n d Numeric field of width n with d decimal places F, Float n d Floating Numeric field of width n with d decimal places Q, Varbinary n - Varbinary field of width n V, Varchar n - Varchar field of width n The [[T13]] and [[T14]] parameters are ignored for W, Y, D, T, G, I, L, and M types. If [[T15]] is not included for the N, F, or B types, the [[T16]] parameter defaults to zero (no decimal places).
**[[T17]] | [[T18]]**
Specifies whether null values are allowed in the field. [[T19]] permits null values, while [[T20]] does not allow null values.
**[[T21]] [[T22]]**
Specifies a validation rule for the field. The [[T23]] parameter must evaluate to a logical expression and can be a user-defined function or a stored procedure.
**[[T24]] [[T25]]**
Specifies an error message. [[T26]] displays this message when the validation rule specified in the [[T27]] clause generates an error. The message displays only when data is changed within a Browse window or Edit window.
**[[T28]] [[[T29]] NextValue [[[T30]] StepValue ]]**
Enables autoincrementing for the field. NextValue specifies the start value and can be a positive or a negative integer value ranging from 2,147,483,647 to -2,147,483,647. The default value is 1. You can set NextValue using the Next Value box on the Fields tab in the Table Designer. StepValue specifies the increment value for the field and can be a positive, nonzero integer value ranging from 1 to 255. The default value is 1. You can set StepValue using the Step box on the Fields tab in the Table Designer. Autoincrementing values cannot be null ([[T31]]). Note Tables containing automatically incrementing field values append table-buffered records approximately 35% slower than tables without automatically incrementing field values, which might affect performance. When using table buffering, the table header is locked when the record is appended.
**[[T32]] [[T33]]**
Specifies a default value for the field. The data type of [[T34]] must be the same as the specified field's data type. If you use the [[T35]] clause to turn on autoincrementing for a field and specify a default value, [[T36]] stores the default value in the table but does not use it. [[T37]] uses the default value if you use the [[T38]] - [[T39]] command to remove autoincrementing for the field.
**[[T40]]**
Creates a candidate index for the field. The candidate index tag has the same name as the field. For more information about candidate indexes, see [[T41]] Index Types .
**[[T42]] [[T43]]**
Specifies a collation sequence other than the default setting, [[T44]]. The [[T45]] parameter must be a valid [[T46]] collation sequence. For more information about setting collation sequences, see Optimizing International Applications and [[T47]] Command .
**[[T48]]**
Prevents translation to a different code page for Character , Memo , and Varchar fields. You can specify [[T49]] only for Character , Memo , and Varchar fields.
**[[T50]] ArrayName**
Specifies the name of an existing array whose contents are the name, type, precision, and scale for each field in the temporary table. You can use the [[T51]] clause instead of specifying individual fields. For the proper format of the contents of the array, see [[T52]] Function . Autoincrementing is turned on when the step value is greater than 0.

You can manipulate a temporary table created with [[T0]] like any other table — you can browse and index it, and you can append and modify records. The temporary table opens in the lowest numbered available (unused) work area and can be accessed by its alias. Each field in the temporary table is defined with a name, type, precision, and scale. These definitions can be obtained from the command itself or from an array. The temporary table opens exclusively, regardless of the setting of [[T1]].

If you omit [[T2]] and [[T3]], the current setting of [[T4]] determines if null values are allowed in the field. However, if you omit [[T5]] and [[T6]] and include the [[T7]] or [[T8]] clause, [[T9]] disregards the current setting of [[T10]], and the field defaults to [[T11]].

Null values and duplicate records are not permitted in a field used for a candidate index. However, [[T12]] does not generate an error if you create a candidate index for a field that supports null values. [[T13]] generates an error if you attempt to enter a null or duplicate value into a field used for a candidate index.

> **Note:** Candidate indexes, created by including the [[T0]] option (provided for [[T1]] compatibility) in [[T2]] – [[T3]] or [[T4]] – [[T5]] commands, are not the same as indexes created in the [[T6]] command with the [[T7]] option. An index created in the [[T8]] command using the [[T9]] option allows duplicate index keys; candidate indexes do not allow duplicate index keys. For more information about the [[T10]] option in the [[T11]] command, see [[T12]] Command .

If the table is converted to another code page, the fields for which [[T13]] has been specified are not translated.

Specifies whether an object is visible or hidden. Read/write at design time and run time.

[[C0]]

**[[T0]]**
Specifies a value that determines whether an object is visible or hidden. The following table lists the values for [[T1]] . [[T2]] Description True ([[T3]]) The object is visible. (Default in the Form Designer) False ([[T4]]) The object is hidden. (Default in program code) Note Even when the object is hidden, you can still access it in code. Tip To hide an object at startup, set the Visible property to False ([[T5]]) at design time. If you set the Visible property in code, you can hide an object and display it at run time in response to a particular event.

Applies To: CheckBox Control | Column Object | ComboBox Control | CommandButton Control | CommandGroup Control | Container Object | Control Object ([[T0]]) | EditBox Control | Form Object | FormSet Object | Grid Control | Image Control ([[T1]]) | Label Control ([[T2]]) | Line Control | ListBox Control | [[T3]] Bound Control | [[T4]] Container Control | OptionButton Control | OptionGroup Control | PageFrame Control | Project Object ([[T5]]) | _SCREEN System Variable | Separator Object | Shape Control | Spinner Control | TextBox Control ([[T6]]) | ToolBar Object

For Form objects, when Visible is set to False ([[T7]]), the form is hidden and the most recently active form set, form, or other object becomes active. When Visible is set to True ([[T8]]), the form becomes visible; however, the form does not become active. To make a form visible and active in the same step, use the Show method. For more information, see Show Method ([[T9]]).

> **Note:** A form in a FormSet object does not display when its Visible property is set to False ([[T10]]) even if the form set's Visible property is set to True ([[T11]]). However, all forms in the form set are hidden if the form set's Visible property is set to False ([[T12]]).

Setting a form's Visible property to True ([[T13]]) does not affect the form's Order property setting.

For Separator objects, the Visible property determines whether a space appears as the separator when its Style property is set to 0 (Normal - do not display a line). For example, when the separator's Visible property is set to True ([[T0]]), and its Style property is set to 0, a space appears instead of the separator. When the separator's Visible property is set to False ([[T1]]), no space appears, regardless of the setting of its Style property.

In versions prior to [[T2]] 5.0, setting the Visible property for the _SCREEN system variable has no effect.
